feedback.reason: The prompt gives independent GPU load and worker failure, which justify isolating compute. Durable job identity must remain under one recoverable owner so the split does not lose accepted work.
feedback.details: Keep one authoritative job record and operation ID. Scale GPU workers independently from interactive request handling, and let leases/recovery consume the durable journal after worker replacement. If the workloads shared failure and scaling needs, a split would add network complexity without benefit; here independent GPU pressure and worker lifecycle make isolation useful.

messages.text: The new boundary has no durable job owner, so accepted work can disappear when the API or worker is replaced.
Co-location alone does not meet the independent capacity and failure requirement.
Two job authorities can start duplicate renditions and disagree about status.
Worker lifecycle is exactly the failure mode the durable job journal must survive.

options.text: Own GPU transcode jobs separately from interactive metadata reads, with durable job status and isolated capacity.
Move orchestration into a separate worker service but leave accepted job state only in the interactive API process.
Keep one service but route GPU work and interactive traffic through the same exhausted worker pool.
Let the API and transcode service each create authoritative job IDs and independently retry missing jobs.
Move both the durable job journal and its ownership to ephemeral workers that restart after each task.

prompt: Video transcoding runs for 25 minutes and consumes GPU, while interactive metadata and playback requests must remain available during worker replacement. The job has a durable journal and can be processed by independent workers. Where should the service boundary sit?

feedback.reason: The decisive requirement is a coordinated five-minute rollback across flag behavior and persisted data. Cohesive ownership makes the decision/audit path accountable, while compatibility remains a required data contract.
feedback.details: Keep the rule decision and audit revision with the owner that controls persisted rollout state, or split only behind a versioned contract that preserves old-reader behavior and rollback. Use additive/dual-readable data during the rollback window and delay destructive changes. Service boundaries do not provide a migration or undo guarantee by themselves.

messages.text: The flag may roll back while persisted data remains unreadable to old clients.
Feature state and stored data are separate; the flag does not restore an incompatible schema.
Different decisions and revisions can diverge, leaving no clear owner of the cohort state.
A single boundary does not make an incompatible migration reversible.

options.text: Keep flag rules and their audit record with the team that owns rollout behavior and compatibility.
Put flag evaluation in one service and schema mutation in another with no coordinated version or rollback contract.
Keep the split but assume setting the flag off automatically reverses the persistence change.
Let both services independently evaluate the rollout rule and write audit records.
Keep one service but perform an irreversible data rewrite before verifying old-reader compatibility.

prompt: A feature rollout rule service and its audit record are maintained by one team. The new flag changes persisted records; turning the flag off must roll back within five minutes while old readers remain active. Should the rule evaluator and persistence/audit owner be split?

feedback.reason: The write invariant requires one transaction owner, while high-volume reads can be isolated if their freshness is explicit. Split the projection, not the conflict check from commit.
feedback.details: The reservation owner atomically enforces no overlap. A separately scaled availability projection may lag up to 10 seconds, so the UI labels its results as candidates and the final write rechecks the invariant. If the prompt did not establish independent read load or tolerated staleness, the extra projection/service would add cost without evidence.

messages.text: The check and commit can race across service boundaries, allowing overlapping bookings.
Independent authorities can both confirm the same resource range before reconciliation.
A 10-second-stale projection is advisory and cannot serialize competing writes.
This preserves ownership but ignores the stated read scaling need; a bounded-stale projection can scale independently.

options.text: Keep slot availability and overlap enforcement in the transactional booking owner.
Put availability checking in a read service and reservation commit in another service without a shared atomic claim.
Allow each booking service instance to maintain its own authoritative slot ledger and reconcile later.
Treat a fresh-enough read projection as the owner of slot reservation and confirm directly from it.
Keep all high-volume availability reads on the transactional write database to avoid a staleness contract.

prompt: Two booking requests can overlap for one resource, and slot ownership is stored in one transactional database. Read availability is high volume and can tolerate 10 seconds of staleness. Which service boundary preserves correctness while scaling reads?

feedback.reason: The index has independent scaling and rebuild needs, while its accepted lag means it is a derived projection. Separate it from source ownership and make replay/freshness observable.
feedback.details: The source writer commits authoritative changes and places durable change data in a replayable stream/log. The index service can scale independently, rebuild from that history, and expose applied watermark/lag up to the 15-second target. Queries must not interpret index lag as source deletion. A projection boundary is appropriate because the source remains authoritative.

messages.text: The projection is allowed to lag and rebuild, so it cannot replace the source of truth.
A service outage would permanently lose updates and prevent the index from catching up.
Temporary projection lag is not evidence of deletion.
The split does not provide independent scaling if its bottleneck remains shared.

options.text: Run indexing as a separate projection with its own write/query budgets and explicit lag.
Move authoritative record writes to the search index and infer source state from indexed documents.
Create a separate index service that receives best-effort updates with no durable change log or replay path.
Treat records absent from the current index as deleted in the source service.
Separate source and index deployments but route both through the same exhausted indexing worker pool.

prompt: Search indexing has independent CPU and storage growth from source writes. Analysts can tolerate up to 15 seconds of index lag, and the index must be rebuildable by replaying source changes. How should service ownership be split?

feedback.reason: The prompt establishes different CPU and latency profiles, so worker isolation is justified. Durable job ownership and budgets are still needed to make the boundary recoverable and bounded.
feedback.details: Keep urgent ingress on a protected short path with reserved capacity. Persist batch plan jobs under one owner and execute them in a separate cost-limited worker pool. Share route data through an explicit versioned contract and ensure planner saturation cannot consume urgent resources. A separate process alone is insufficient if CPU or downstream capacity remains shared.

messages.text: A process/service boundary does not isolate a shared saturated resource.
The urgent 100 ms path becomes dependent on minutes-long computations.
Divergent route authorities can send dispatch using stale or conflicting plans.
Independent scaling does not remove capacity limits; unbounded work can still exhaust planner resources and downstream dependencies.

options.text: Isolate bursty batch planning from urgent dispatch while keeping a reserved urgent lane.
Deploy a separate planner service but let it consume the same CPU and worker pool as urgent dispatch.
Route urgent dispatch through the durable planner queue and wait behind batch work.
Let planner and dispatcher maintain separate authoritative route versions and reconcile after dispatch.
Separate planner workers but accept unlimited expensive jobs into them.

prompt: Route planning consumes bursty CPU for several minutes; urgent dispatch ingress must meet a 100 ms deadline and should remain available during planner saturation. The planner can use durable jobs. Which boundary reduces contention?

feedback.reason: The provider adapter has an independent failure mode, but payment intent identity and reconciliation must remain authoritative in one owner. A split is safe only when the same identity crosses it.
feedback.details: Payment service owns one intent bound to amount/parameters and its pending/unknown/final state. An adapter may isolate provider credentials, concurrency, and outage policy, but receives that same intent identity and returns a reconcilable result. Checkout never creates a second charge just because adapter status is missing. If independent failure isolation were not needed, the extra service boundary could be unnecessary.

messages.text: Separate identities can cause duplicate provider charges when outcomes are ambiguous.
A timeout can hide a successful charge; missing local status is not proof of provider failure.
The stated independent outage/rate needs are unresolved.
The boundary loses the information needed to retry and reconcile the original charge.

options.text: Keep payment intent state and reconciliation in one owner; isolate provider-specific calls behind an adapter.
Let both checkout and provider-adapter services create their own charge IDs for one customer intent.
Move status ownership to the provider adapter and let checkout treat missing adapter state as failed.
Keep a shared provider adapter with no rate isolation so one provider outage blocks every payment path.
Separate the adapter and payment service but pass no stable operation identity or reconciliation status between them.

prompt: Payment intent state must survive provider timeouts and be reconciled before a new charge. The provider adapter has its own outage pattern and needs independent rate limits. Where should the service boundary be?

feedback.reason: Durable admission is the promise made to the caller; analysis may scale independently only after that promise is recorded under a stable case identity.
feedback.details: The accountable fraud owner persists the high-risk case and returns accepted only after that write is durable. Analysis workers consume the case by stable ID and update its status. Capacity isolation can protect admission from slow analysis, but the bridge must retain acceptance proof and provide replay/recovery. A best-effort handoff does not meet the promise.

messages.text: A message loss after the ACK makes the high-risk case disappear.
The caller was promised acceptance before an accountable owner persisted the case.
Separate identities can create duplicate reviews or make one case untraceable.
The slow analysis workload can block the time-sensitive admission path.

options.text: Own durable high-risk admission separately from scalable evidence analysis, with acknowledgment after persistence.
Return accepted from the gateway and send the case to analysis through a best-effort message.
Let slow analysis workers decide whether the original admission succeeded after the caller has already received success.
Have gateway and analysis services independently create case identities and retry missing cases.
Keep durable admission and slow analysis in one saturated worker pool, so analysis delays acceptance.

prompt: High-risk fraud admission must be durable before the caller receives accepted. Slow evidence analysis can scale separately and may finish later. Which ownership boundary preserves accountability?

feedback.reason: Compute load can scale independently, but artifact meaning depends on one pinned export identity and input snapshot. Keep that state under one owner and let workers render from it.
feedback.details: The export owner records period, snapshot cutoff, rules revision, and exportId before accepting work. Render workers may scale/retry separately, but they consume those immutable inputs and publish one completed artifact for that ID. Later corrections create a new export identity. A service split without pinned inputs makes retries nondeterministic.

messages.text: The same identity can produce different bytes after a correction, breaking audit reproducibility.
The worker cannot reproduce the accepted export because its inputs are not pinned.
Heavy computation can starve interactive traffic despite having an async boundary.
Multiple completion authorities can race and overwrite the canonical output.

options.text: Own immutable export identity and snapshot rules with payroll; scale rendering workers behind the job boundary.
Let each worker reread current payroll data when a retry starts and overwrite the artifact for the same export ID.
Move rendering to a separate service but pass only a period, with no source cutoff or rules revision.
Run minute-long export rendering in the same request workers that serve payroll reads and writes.
Let the request service and renderer each decide export completion and publish whichever artifact finishes last.

prompt: Payroll export requests can be accepted quickly, while rendering takes minutes. A retry must return the same bytes for the same period and rules revision; compute workers need independent scaling. Which service boundary is appropriate?

feedback.reason: The report cutoff must be shared even if read projections scale independently. One snapshot identity anchors the calculation; watermarks make tolerated lag visible.
feedback.details: The report owner selects an immutable cutoff/snapshot and binds all aggregate reads to it. Projections may be separated for load if they can serve that version and report their applied watermark within the 10-second freshness contract. Do not combine independently latest values as one report. If a projection cannot prove the cutoff, use the authoritative source or report unavailable/stale.

messages.text: Different cutoffs can yield a total that never existed at one point in time.
The caller cannot tell whether the report uses a coherent cutoff or exceeds the freshness allowance.
Independent cutoffs can drift and cannot guarantee one internally consistent report.
This avoids projection lag but ignores the established read scaling/freshness contract.

options.text: Build reports as a bounded read projection over source-owned aggregates at one declared cutoff.
Let each reporting service read its own latest table state and combine results under one report ID.
Scale projections separately but discard source version and watermark to simplify the API.
Have every report service independently choose and label a cutoff without a shared snapshot identity.
Force every scalable read through one source database despite the stated projection tolerance and independent read load.

prompt: Financial reports join several source aggregates. Reads can scale independently and tolerate a declared 10-second projection lag, but each report must use one immutable cutoff. Where should data and read ownership be placed?

feedback.reason: The two workloads have distinct capacity needs and a bounded freshness budget. Separate their admission resources and use a durable, bounded bridge with observable lag.
feedback.details: Give producer ingress its own bounded buffer/backpressure and protect the analyst query pool. Persist accepted events for replay, and expose queue age/applied watermark; if lag exceeds two seconds, report it explicitly. A durable queue is not enough when it is unbounded or when its consumer shares the query pool.

messages.text: The service split does not isolate the actual shared bottleneck.
An ingest outage can lose accepted measurements before the query projection receives them.
The query path competes with burst ingestion and has no bounded freshness or latency guarantee.
Durability without a bound hides overload and misrepresents unprocessed data as available.

options.text: Split telemetry ingestion from interactive query capacity while retaining explicit durability and watermark contracts.
Deploy ingest and query as separate services but connect both to the same saturated worker and connection pool.
Separate the services but use best-effort event delivery with no durable buffer or replay.
Serve analyst queries directly from the ingestion queue while producers write without backpressure.
Use a durable queue with no capacity or age limit and report queries as current regardless of backlog.

prompt: Telemetry producers burst to 50,000 events per second, while analysts issue interactive queries with a 250 ms target. Each workload needs separate capacity; a durable bridge may delay ingestion up to two seconds. What boundary fits?

feedback.reason: Providers fail and scale independently, so worker/adapters can be isolated. Durable intent and bounded calls preserve the accepted-delivery and request-budget contracts.
feedback.details: Persist delivery ID and status before the gateway acknowledges. Run provider-specific workers with deadlines, in-flight caps, and bounded retry ownership; keep each provider’s breaker scoped. The gateway need not wait for provider completion. A split service without durable state or limits merely relocates the same failure.

messages.text: A slow dependency can exhaust the gateway before its 500 ms budget is met.
A gateway restart loses accepted work despite the worker service still existing.
Independent provider failures become a shared outage rather than an isolated dependency fault.
A service boundary without concurrency/retry bounds can still exhaust provider and worker capacity.

options.text: Isolate slow provider calls in delivery workers behind a durable notification gateway handoff.
Call every provider inline in the shared gateway worker and wait up to each provider’s full timeout.
Move provider calls to a worker service but keep accepted delivery state only in gateway memory.
Combine all providers behind one global circuit breaker and stop all notifications when any provider fails.
Use separate provider workers but allow unlimited in-flight calls and retries.

prompt: Notification providers fail independently and can be slow. The gateway must keep its 500 ms request budget, while accepted deliveries survive process restarts and remain queryable. What service boundary should be used?

feedback.reason: The write path has a trust and retention boundary; search scaling can be separated only as a derived, authorized view. The ledger remains the source for replay.
feedback.details: Authenticate the actor at one append authority and persist an integrity-protected immutable event under the seven-year retention policy. The search service consumes/rebuilds a projection but enforces tenant/role authorization and cannot rewrite the ledger. At retention expiry, use an audited purge policy. Separate read scaling does not justify moving provenance or retention ownership.

messages.text: The service boundary loses the provenance that must be bound to every record.
Independent writers can alter accepted history and bypass retention/integrity policy.
A projection can be rebuilt or lag; it cannot replace the durable append and retention owner.
Immutability does not override the stated seven-year retention and access policy.

options.text: Keep authenticated immutable audit append and retention under a trust boundary; scale authorized reads separately.
Move audit appends to a separate service that accepts actorId from any caller and has no trusted principal context.
Let write and search services update or delete the same audit rows directly for convenience.
Treat the scalable search projection as the immutable authority and rebuild the source ledger from its current documents.
Make the ledger immutable by retaining every entry forever with unrestricted access.

prompt: Audit writes require authenticated actor identity, immutable append, and a declared seven-year retention policy. Search queries may scale separately, but readers must see only authorized records. Where should boundaries be placed?

feedback.reason: Ingestion and projection have distinct replay/read roles, but monotonic state needs one writer. A service split is safe only with stable event identity and source revision.
feedback.details: Persist authenticated carrier events with stable IDs in a replayable log. A single projection writer consumes them and atomically compares each revision with current state before applying. The read model can scale independently; lower revisions are ignored or quarantined. Splitting services without a monotonic owner or replay path creates stale/regressing views.

messages.text: Different replicas can apply out-of-order events inconsistently and regress shipment state.
An outage or retry loss prevents replay and may leave current state permanently stale.
Co-location does not fix out-of-order updates; the revision guard remains necessary.
Two sources of truth can disagree about the latest state.

options.text: Keep carrier event ordering at ingestion and expose a revision-guarded shipment projection for customer reads.
Let each projection replica decide which event is newest using local arrival time and overwrite the shared state.
Send carrier events to the projection by best-effort message and discard them after first delivery attempt.
Keep ingestion and projection together but overwrite current state on every delivered event.
Let ingestion and projection services both own the authoritative current shipment record.

prompt: Carrier ingestion receives out-of-order updates, while customers query the current shipment state. The event log must support replay; the projection must never regress below revision 42. What boundaries should be separated?

feedback.reason: Processing can scale separately, but one durable intent identity must own the billable effect and its reconciliation. The boundary preserves that identity end to end.
feedback.details: Persist an operation ID and parameter binding before acceptance. Workers can be replaced and retried, but they pass the same idempotency identity to the billable provider and update one durable job record. Reconcile unknown outcomes before another charge. Independent workers improve scaling; they do not justify independent operation identities.

messages.text: Different identities make one intent appear as two billable operations.
Worker replacement can lose accepted intent or repeat a charge without a reconciliation record.
The adapter cannot reliably reconcile a response lost before it learns which intent to query.
Long extraction work can exhaust interactive capacity, despite an independent worker scaling need.

options.text: Keep billable intent identity and provider charge guard with the extraction owner; scale workers behind durable jobs.
Let the API and worker service each generate a new provider charge ID when they retry the same client request.
Move processing to independent workers but keep no durable accepted job or side-effect record.
Let the provider adapter decide whether the client intent exists, without a stable operation ID from the API.
Keep billable processing in the interactive API pool so no explicit job handoff is needed.

prompt: Document extraction has a billable provider call. The client may retry after a lost response, and processing workers need independent scaling. The extraction must charge once per user intent. Which boundary is appropriate?

feedback.reason: Inventory correctness belongs to one atomic owner; presentation can scale separately if it reflects durable state and does not allocate itself.
feedback.details: The inventory owner performs an atomic claim and records a stable allocation ID. A status service/projection may present accepted, pending, confirmed, or failed as the operation progresses; it never becomes a second allocator. Confirm only after the authoritative claim. If allocation is still uncertain, status remains pending/unknown rather than triggering a new attempt.

messages.text: Two services can allocate the same seat before reconciliation.
The cross-service gap allows concurrent requests to both pass the check.
A status projection cannot claim the seat before the inventory owner commits it.
A read-only status request would create repeated allocations and duplicate side effects.

options.text: Keep seat reservation atomicity in inventory; let ticket presentation own only the async client-facing status.
Let the presentation service assign seats from its own copy of inventory and notify the inventory service afterward.
Put seat availability in one service and final reservation in another with no atomic claim protocol.
Treat a pending status view as proof the seat has been reserved and issue a ticket immediately.
Have every status refresh call the allocator again when state is pending.

prompt: Ticket sales have one authoritative seat inventory. Reservation must be atomic, but the presentation layer may take several seconds to show a user the final result. What service boundary preserves the seat invariant and a truthful status?

feedback.reason: Search load can be isolated, but tenant access must remain enforced by an authoritative owner and projection lag must be visible.
feedback.details: Derive tenant scope from authenticated identity and apply it server-side before/within the search query. The index is a derived projection with replay and an applied watermark; expose staleness within the 10-second contract. For sensitive case access, revalidate current ownership at the source boundary when needed. A lagging index alone cannot authorize data.

messages.text: The index has already disclosed unauthorized records before client filtering.
A stale projection cannot safely replace the source owner’s current authorization decision.
The caller cannot know whether a missing case is absent or delayed in the projection.
This preserves authorization but does not address the separate query scaling need; a scoped projection can do so safely.

options.text: Keep case authorization at the tenant-aware source owner; scale search as a scoped projection.
Let the search service query all tenants and rely on the UI to hide records outside the current tenant.
Move access ownership into a lagging index that may not yet reflect a case transfer or revocation.
Scale the index separately but return results without an applied watermark or stale state.
Route all search traffic to the source owner and ignore the stated independent search load.

prompt: Support search is tenant-scoped. The source case owner enforces access, while the search index may scale independently and lag by 10 seconds. How should service boundaries protect privacy and freshness?

feedback.reason: The source owns metadata truth; projections may scale independently only if callers can see freshness and distinguish absence from failure.
feedback.details: Persist asset metadata at one source authority. Cache/search services can serve bounded-stale reads and report as-of age. Return not-found only when source absence is known; report stale/not-yet-indexed or unavailable separately. Rebuildable projections must not claim source ownership or turn temporary lag into deletion.

messages.text: An expiring projection cannot be the durable source of truth.
Projection lag is not proof that the source asset does not exist.
Callers cannot distinguish source absence from projection or dependency failure.
This ignores the established read load; projections can help if their freshness and result semantics are explicit.

options.text: Keep metadata writes with the source owner and serve scalable reads from a projection with explicit freshness.
Move the authoritative metadata record into a cache that can expire or be rebuilt independently.
Return confirmed missing whenever a separate projection has no current entry.
Create separate source and cache services but let each return its own undocumented 404/503 behavior.
Force every read through the source database despite independent cache/search scaling needs.

prompt: Media metadata source writes are authoritative. A cache/search projection can scale separately but may be stale or unavailable; callers must distinguish confirmed missing, stale, and service failure. Where should the metadata boundary sit?

feedback.reason: The transport can redeliver, but only the effect owner knows whether actuation occurred. One stable identity lets gateway retries and device-side dedup refer to the same command.
feedback.details: Persist command acceptance and delivery attempts at the gateway under one ID. The device records that ID/sequence at the actuation boundary, returns its prior result on replay, and distinguishes accepted from executed. If it may have acted before losing a response, status remains unknown until reconciled; the gateway must not create a fresh action ID. Keep transport and effect semantics separate.

messages.text: The gateway cannot know the physical effect completed when its response was lost; replay protection must reach the actuation boundary.
Delivery acknowledgment proves transport progress, not actuator state.
A replay becomes a new action and can repeat the unsafe physical effect.
Two effect authorities can conflict and cannot provide one coherent execution result.

options.text: Keep device sequence/dedup and physical actuation outcome with the device-facing owner; report delivery separately.
Deduplicate only at the gateway and assume a device that acted before a lost response will not act again.
Treat successful message delivery as proof the device performed the physical action.
Generate a new command identity on every reconnect so each delivery attempt is independently accepted.
Let gateway and device each independently decide whether a command should actuate.

prompt: IoT command delivery and device actuation have separate failure modes: the gateway may redeliver after reconnect, while a device may act and lose its response. Duplicate physical action is unsafe. Which boundary should own each guarantee?
